opus-5.5.text:
I think frustration is almost the default state of being a researcher. If you're doing research that actually matters, most of the time you're failing. You have an idea, you think it's beautiful, you run the experiments, and it doesn't work. Or it works a little, but not in the way you hoped. That happens again and again, and I think anyone who has done research for a while knows that feeling very well.

For me, there are a few layers to it. The first is the everyday frustration: the experiments don't work, the numbers don't go up, the paper gets rejected. Those things hurt, especially when you're a student, because you feel like your whole identity is tied to that one project. But over time I've come to see that this kind of frustration is actually a signal that you're working on something nontrivial. If everything worked on the first try, it probably wasn't a very interesting question.

The second layer is deeper, and I think it's more specific to our field right now. AI moves so fast. You might spend a year on a direction, and then a big lab releases something with ten thousand times your compute, and suddenly it feels like your work doesn't matter anymore. There's a kind of existential anxiety there: what is the role of an individual researcher, or an academic lab, when scale seems to solve everything? I've felt that many times.

The way I deal with it is to try to separate taste from outcomes. You can't control whether a specific experiment works, or whether someone scoops you. But you can control what questions you think are important and how honestly you pursue them. If I believe a question is fundamental, like how visual representation should be learned, or what world models really need, then a failed experiment is just information. It tells me something about the problem.

And I also think it's important to remember that research is a long game. Many ideas that were dismissed at one point came back years later and became central. So frustration, in a way, is part of the price of being early. If you're doing what everyone else agrees is right, you'll feel less frustrated, but you probably also won't find anything new.

So I try to treat it not as something to eliminate, but as something to live with, and maybe even appreciate a little. It means you're still pushing on something you don't fully understand yet. That's kind of the whole point.

r001.rationale: The response describes repeated failures and uncertainty, but does not explain frustration as coming from exploring without a clear sense of direction.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss joy or state that joyful moments are only a small part of a researcher’s experience.

r003.rationale: It mentions AI-related anxiety, but not increased discussion during the AI wave or how that discussion makes researchers feel less alone.

fable-5.1.text:
Frustration is honestly the default state of being a researcher. I'd say ninety-five percent of the time, things don't work. You have an idea, you think it's beautiful, you run the experiment, and the numbers come back and they're just flat. Or worse, your baseline is stronger than your method. That's most days.

I think early on I misunderstood this. I thought the frustration meant I was doing something wrong, or that I wasn't good enough. Now I see it differently. The frustration is actually the signal that you're working on something real. If everything worked on the first try, it probably means the problem was too easy, or someone had already solved it and you just didn't know.

The other thing I've learned is that the frustration comes in different flavors, and you have to tell them apart. There's the frustration of the experiment failing, which is fine, that's just information. Then there's the frustration of not knowing what question to ask, which is much harder. In the first case you just need to be patient and keep debugging. In the second case, you need to step back and think, maybe talk to people, read things outside your area.

And then there's a third kind, which is the frustration that comes from the field itself. Right now everything moves so fast. You work on something for six months and then a paper comes out that does a similar thing, or a big lab scales it up and your results look small by comparison. That one is hard, especially for students. I tell my students that you can't control timing, you can only control whether you understood something deeply. If you understood it, that knowledge stays with you even if the paper doesn't get the attention.

So I guess my understanding is that you shouldn't try to eliminate the frustration. You should try to build a relationship with it. The researchers I admire most aren't the ones who never get stuck. They're the ones who stay curious while they're stuck. That's a skill, and I think it's maybe the most important one.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes frustration from failed experiments and from not knowing what question to ask, but it does not explain it as exploring without a clear sense of direction.

r002.rationale: It says things fail 95% of the time, but does not state that moments of joy occupy only a small fraction of the experience.

r003.rationale: It mentions the field moving quickly and talks about discussing ideas with people, but does not say that discussion during the current AI wave reduces the feeling of exploring alone.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of the frustration comes from the gap between how much effort you put in and how little certainty you get back. You can work very hard on an idea, run the experiments carefully, and still find that it doesn’t work. Effort doesn’t guarantee a result, and that can be difficult to accept.

There are also two different questions that can get mixed together: “Is this idea working?” and “Am I a good researcher?” When an experiment fails, it’s very easy to hear it as an answer to the second question. But usually it’s only telling you something about a particular hypothesis, under particular conditions.

For me, the useful thing is to make the frustration more specific. What did I expect? What actually happened? Is there something I can test next? You don’t have to pretend that failure feels good. But if you can turn that feeling into a clearer question, you have a way to keep moving.

And sometimes you need to step away. Persistence matters, but so does recognizing when you’re repeating yourself rather than learning. Developing that judgment is part of becoming a researcher.

r001.rationale: The response attributes frustration to uncertain outcomes despite effort, but does not explain it as exploring without a clear sense of direction.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that joyful moments are only a small fraction of researchers’ experience.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention the current AI wave, increased discussion, or reduced feelings of exploring alone.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of the frustration comes from the gap between having an intuition and being able to show that it’s right. You might feel that an idea makes sense, but the experiment doesn’t work. And then you have to ask: Is the idea wrong? Is there a bug? Am I asking the wrong question? You don’t necessarily know which one it is.

That uncertainty is part of research. If every step were clear and every experiment worked, you would probably be implementing something we already understood. But knowing that intellectually doesn’t make a failed experiment feel good.

For me, the useful thing is to turn frustration into a more specific question. What did this result actually tell me? What can I test next to distinguish between the possible explanations? Sometimes you keep going, and sometimes you have to let go of an idea you really liked. Developing that judgment—being persistent without becoming attached—is one of the hardest parts of being a researcher.

r001.rationale: The response links frustration to uncertainty about whether an idea, experiment, or question is on the right track, conveying the lack of clear direction while exploring.

r002.rationale: It acknowledges that failed experiments feel bad, but does not say that joyful moments make up only a small fraction of research.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss the current AI wave, increased discussion, or feeling less alone in exploration.
